payload.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Court Of Small Causes Bengaluru
payload.holding: The tribunal held that the insurer proved a fundamental breach of policy conditions due to the driver lacking a valid driving licence, but directed the insurer to pay the compensation to the petitioner in the first instance under the 'pay and recover' principle, with liberty to recover the same from the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Punjab & Haryana At Chandigarh
payload.holding: The criminal revision petition is partly allowed by upholding the conviction of the petitioner under Sections 279, 337, 304-A, and 427 of the IPC, but modifying the substantive sentence for the offence under Section 304-A IPC from two years of rigorous imprisonment to 18 months, while maintaining the other sentences and fine.

args.question: What precedents could the insurance company use AGAINST our client, where the driver had no valid licence? Assess how damaging each one is.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: This is a Supreme Court judgment that directly protects third-party claimants. It holds that even where the driver lacked the proper licence endorsement, the insurer must pay the third party. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not the claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest Supreme Court authority in the corpus for the proposition that a licence defect does not defeat a third-party claim. It directly counters the insurer's 'no licence = no liability' argument.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Delhi High Court held that even where the driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence while driving a goods vehicle (commercial), the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. This directly supports our client's right to receive compensation despite any licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Lehru, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties is not defeated by licence breaches.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor and recover from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Karnataka Full Bench decision is the most comprehensive analysis in the corpus. It holds that even a 'fundamental breach' (breach that caused the accident) does not allow the insurer to avoid paying the third party. The only exception is fraud/collusion between the victim and insured — which is not our case.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench judgment that squarely rejects the insurer's argument that a fundamental licence breach absolves them of all liability to third parties. It provides the strongest ratio for our position.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach (that is breach of condition which is the cause for the accident) and the insurer proves the said breach.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and then recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab). The court still ordered pay-and-recover. This supports our client's right to payment despite any licence class mismatch.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Madras High Court judgment applies Swaran Singh and confirms that even where the insurer proves the driver was not 'duly licensed' for the specific vehicle class, the third-party claimant still gets paid first.
supporting.quote: the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimant and recover the same subsequently from the insured. The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence with transport endorsement but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court still ordered pay-and-recover. This supports our client's position regardless of the specific licence deficiency.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Madras High Court judgment applies S.Iyyapan (Supreme Court) and confirms that the insurer's statutory duty to third parties overrides licence class deficiencies.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for hazardous goods. The court still ordered pay-and-recover, not exoneration. This supports our client's right to payment.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even for the most serious licence deficiency (missing mandatory special endorsement for hazardous goods), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not denial to the third party.
supporting.quote: the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period; however, the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired and was renewed after the accident. The court still ordered pay-and-recover. This supports our client even if the driver had no valid licence at the time of accident.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly adverse fact pattern for our client (licence expired, not valid on accident date), yet the court still protected the third-party claimant with pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner to protect third-party rights.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no licence at all. The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover. This is the strongest supporting precedent for our client where the driver had absolutely no licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the most extreme case — driver with no licence whatsoever — the tribunal applied pay-and-recover. This directly defeats the insurer's argument that 'no licence = no liability.'
supporting.quote: the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time. ... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability, especially where the breach did not contribute to causing the accident.
supporting.fact_alignment: The drivers' licences had expired but were renewed later. The court held the insurers jointly liable with the owners. This supports our client even where the licence had lapsed.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment introduces the 'contribution to accident' test — if the licence defect did not cause the accident, it is not a fundamental breach. This is an additional argument our counsel can deploy.
supporting.quote: the non-renewal of the licence as on the date of the accident cannot be said to have contributed to the causing of the accident. Where the breach alleged is not a factor which has contributed to the causing of the accident, the said breach would not be a fundamental breach.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this for the proposition that a fake driving licence is an absolute defence. However, this case is about own-damage claims (insured v. insurer), not third-party claims. The Supreme Court expressly held that Swaran Singh 'has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Since our client is a third-party claimant, this judgment actually supports us — para 3 of the holding says 'in case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.'
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims. For third-party claims (our case), the same judgment states: 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.' The insurer cannot use this against a third-party claimant.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, and the insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite the tribunal's finding that 'no liability can be fastened upon Insurance Company' and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability.' However, the same tribunal then ordered pay-and-recover, so the third-party claimant still gets paid. The insurer's argument will be that they are not liable at all, but the order itself contradicts that.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Despite the strong language about the insurer being 'absolved,' the tribunal ultimately ordered pay-and-recover. The third-party claimant received full compensation. The insurer's 'absolved' language refers to its relationship with the insured, not with the third-party claimant. The operative order protects the claimant.
adverse.quote: the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability. ... However, under the principle of 'Pay and Recovery' the respondent No.2 is directed to pay the award amount with accrued interest thereon to the petitioner.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving licence and without wearing a helmet.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that driving without a licence amounts to contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation. However, this case involved the injured claimant himself driving without a licence (he was the rider of the motorcycle), not a third-party victim hit by an unlicensed driver. The contributory negligence finding was based on the claimant's own unlawful act, not the driver's licence status.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the injured claimant himself was the unlicensed driver. In our case, our client is a third-party victim (or dependent of a deceased victim) who had no control over the driver's licence status. The principle that a victim's own lack of licence can constitute contributory negligence does not extend to penalising an innocent third party for the driver's licence defect.
adverse.quote: the injured Kamal ... did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant but has a right to recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: This is actually a supporting precedent (pay-and-recover was ordered), but the insurer may cite it for the proposition that the tribunal found 'no valid licence with the driver.' The risk is low because the court still ordered pay-and-recover in the claimant's favour.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court expressly rejected the insurer's argument that 'once learned Tribunal found that there was no valid driving license ... there could not have been any occasion for the learned Tribunal to direct the insurance company to pay.' The court upheld the pay-and-recover order. This supports our client.
adverse.quote: learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

adverse.title: L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav
adverse.principle: The insurance company must prove that the driving licence was fake and that the owner had knowledge of the fake licence to establish a fundamental breach.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this for the proposition that if they can prove the licence was fake AND the owner knew it, they may avoid liability. However, the court in this very case held the insurer liable because they failed to prove owner knowledge. The burden of proof is on the insurer — a high evidentiary bar.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment actually helps our client. It sets a high bar for the insurer: they must prove not just that the licence was fake, but also that the owner knew it was fake and still permitted the driver to drive. The court cited Hind Samachar (2025 INSC 1204) requiring the insurer to 'bring out the absence of due diligence in the employment of the driver.' If the insurer cannot meet this burden, they remain fully liable.
adverse.quote: the Insurance Company could not prove on record that the factum of fake license was within the knowledge of the owner of the offending vehicle and despite knowledge he permitted the driver to drive the said vehicle. Hence, the insurance company could not prove the fundamental breach of policy.

priority_arguments: The insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149(1) MV Act is not defeated by any breach of policy conditions — the remedy is pay-and-recover, not denial to the claimant (doc_025, doc_033, doc_024).
The Supreme Court in S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and the consistent line of authority from Swaran Singh onwards hold that the insurer must pay the third party first regardless of licence defects.

Even where the driver had no licence at all (doc_024), or an expired licence (doc_003, doc_034), or the wrong class of licence (doc_035, doc_027, doc_001), the courts uniformly ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
The only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025) — which is not our case.
The insurer bears the heavy burden of proving both the licence defect AND the owner's knowledge/wilful breach (doc_005, citing Hind Samachar 2025 INSC 1204).
If the licence defect did not contribute to causing the accident, it is not a 'fundamental breach' at all (doc_034).
Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) — the only insurer-favouring judgment — is expressly limited to own-damage claims and actually confirms the pay-and-recover rule for third-party claims.
strategy.compensation_range: Full compensation as per Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework, without any deduction for licence breach. The only potential deduction is if the insurer proves contributory negligence on the facts (doc_009 is distinguishable — it involved the claimant himself driving without a licence).
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The licence defect does not reduce the quantum of compensation payable to the third-party claimant. The insurer must pay the full awarded amount and then seek recovery from the insured owner separately. Quantum should be computed under the standard Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework based on the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents.
risks: If our client was himself driving without a licence at the time of the accident (rather than being a passenger/pedestrian), the insurer may argue contributory negligence under doc_009, potentially reducing compensation by up to 50%.
If the insurer can prove fraud or collusion between our client and the vehicle owner (doc_025), they could be completely absolved — but this is a very high bar and unlikely on standard facts.
If this is an own-damage claim (property damage to the vehicle itself) rather than a third-party injury/death claim, Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) applies and the insurer may avoid liability entirely.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Proceed under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. The claim should be for third-party injury/death compensation. If the insurer raises the licence defence, cite the consistent line of authority (doc_032, doc_033, doc_025, doc_024) for pay-and-recover. Oppose any attempt to deduct compensation on licence grounds.

caveats: This analysis assumes our client is a third-party claimant (victim or dependent of a deceased victim) who was not driving the offending vehicle. If our client was the driver of the offending vehicle who lacked a licence, doc_009 (Kamal) may apply to reduce compensation for contributory negligence.
This analysis assumes the claim is for third-party injury/death. If the claim is for own-damage (vehicle damage), doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) applies and the insurer may avoid liability entirely.

priority_arguments: The insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149(1) MV Act is not defeated by any breach of policy conditions — the remedy is pay-and-recover, not denial to the claimant (doc_025, doc_033, doc_024).
The Supreme Court in S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and the consistent line of authority from Swaran Singh onwards hold that the insurer must pay the third party first regardless of licence defects.

Even where the driver had no licence at all (doc_024), or an expired licence (doc_003, doc_034), or the wrong class of licence (doc_035, doc_027, doc_001), the courts uniformly ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
The only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025) — which is not our case.
The insurer bears the heavy burden of proving both the licence defect AND the owner's knowledge/wilful breach (doc_005, citing Hind Samachar 2025 INSC 1204).
If the licence defect did not contribute to causing the accident, it is not a 'fundamental breach' at all (doc_034).
Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) — the only insurer-favouring judgment — is expressly limited to own-damage claims and actually confirms the pay-and-recover rule for third-party claims.
strategy.compensation_range: Full compensation as per Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework, without any deduction for licence breach. The only potential deduction is if the insurer proves contributory negligence on the facts (doc_009 is distinguishable — it involved the claimant himself driving without a licence).
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The licence defect does not reduce the quantum of compensation payable to the third-party claimant. The insurer must pay the full awarded amount and then seek recovery from the insured owner separately. Quantum should be computed under the standard Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework based on the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents.
risks: If our client was himself driving without a licence at the time of the accident (rather than being a passenger/pedestrian), the insurer may argue contributory negligence under doc_009, potentially reducing compensation by up to 50%.
If the insurer can prove fraud or collusion between our client and the vehicle owner (doc_025), they could be completely absolved — but this is a very high bar and unlikely on standard facts.
If this is an own-damage claim (property damage to the vehicle itself) rather than a third-party injury/death claim, Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) applies and the insurer may avoid liability entirely.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Proceed under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. The claim should be for third-party injury/death compensation. If the insurer raises the licence defence, cite the consistent line of authority (doc_032, doc_033, doc_025, doc_024) for pay-and-recover. Oppose any attempt to deduct compensation on licence grounds.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — This judgment is about a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes (carrying bricks/iron rods for construction). The insurer was exonerated because the vehicle was used for a purpose not covered by the policy. It has nothing to do with the driver's licence. The insurer cannot use it against a licence-defence claim.

doc_014 (Shivlal) — This judgment is about a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle under the 1939 Act. The insurer was exonerated because the risk of gratuitous passengers is not statutorily required to be covered. It has nothing to do with the driver's licence. Not relevant.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — This judgment is about passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire/reward. The court held they are not 'third parties' under the Act policy and pay-and-recover cannot be ordered. The ratio turns on the claimant's status (gratuitous passenger), not on licence defects. Our client is a genuine third party (pedestrian/other vehicle occupant), so this is distinguishable. The insurer cannot use it against a third-party claimant.

doc_030 (Dadapeera) — This judgment is about a person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor. The court held such a person is not a 'third party' entitled to pay-and-recover because the breach (travelling on mud-guard) is not one of the defences listed in Section 149(2). Critically, the court expressly notes that licence breach IS a defence under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) — 'a condition excluding driving by... any person who is not duly licensed.' So this judgment actually supports the proposition that where the breach IS a licence defect, pay-and-recover IS available. Not adverse.

doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal cases about rash and negligent driving. They address licence absence as a criminal offence under Section 181 MV Act but do not deal with insurance liability or compensation. Not relevant to the insurance defence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant but has a right to recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the proposition that the tribunal found 'no valid licence with the driver.' The risk is low because the court still ordered pay-and-recover in the claimant's favour. The insurer's argument that 'once no valid licence was found, there could be no occasion to direct the insurer to pay' was expressly rejected.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court expressly rejected the insurer's argument and upheld the pay-and-recover order. This supports our client, not the insurer.
adverse.quote: learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

adverse.title: L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav
adverse.principle: The insurance company must prove that the driving licence was fake AND that the owner had knowledge of the fake licence to establish a fundamental breach.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this for the proposition that if they can prove the licence was fake AND the owner knew it, they may avoid liability. However, the court in this very case held the insurer liable because they failed to prove owner knowledge. The burden of proof is on the insurer — a high evidentiary bar.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment actually helps our client. It sets a high bar for the insurer: they must prove not just that the licence was fake, but also that the owner knew it was fake and still permitted the driver to drive. The court cited Hind Samachar (2025 INSC 1204) requiring the insurer to 'bring out the absence of due diligence in the employment of the driver.' If the insurer cannot meet this burden, they remain fully liable.

priority_arguments: The insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149(1) MV Act is not defeated by any breach of policy conditions — the remedy is pay-and-recover, not denial to the claimant (doc_025, doc_033, doc_024).
The Supreme Court in S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and the consistent line of authority from Swaran Singh onwards hold that the insurer must pay the third party first regardless of licence defects.

Even where the driver had no licence at all (doc_024), or an expired licence (doc_003, doc_034), or the wrong class of licence (doc_035, doc_027, doc_001), the courts uniformly ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
The only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025) — which is not our case.
The insurer bears the heavy burden of proving both the licence defect AND the owner's knowledge/wilful breach (doc_005, citing Hind Samachar 2025 INSC 1204).
If the licence defect did not contribute to causing the accident, it is not a 'fundamental breach' at all (doc_034).
Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) — the only insurer-favouring judgment — is expressly limited to own-damage claims and actually confirms the pay-and-recover rule for third-party claims.
strategy.compensation_range: Full compensation as per Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework, without any deduction for licence breach. The only potential deduction is if the insurer proves contributory negligence on the facts (doc_009 is distinguishable — it involved the claimant himself driving without a licence).
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The licence defect does not reduce the quantum of compensation payable to the third-party claimant. The insurer must pay the full awarded amount and then seek recovery from the insured owner separately. Quantum should be computed under the standard Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework based on the deceased's income, age, and number of dependents.
risks: If our client was himself driving without a licence at the time of the accident (rather than being a passenger/pedestrian), the insurer may argue contributory negligence under doc_009, potentially reducing compensation by up to 50%.
If the insurer can prove fraud or collusion between our client and the vehicle owner (doc_025), they could be completely absolved — but this is a very high bar and unlikely on standard facts.
If this is an own-damage claim (property damage to the vehicle itself) rather than a third-party injury/death claim, Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) applies and the insurer may avoid liability entirely.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Proceed under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. The claim should be for third-party injury/death compensation. If the insurer raises the licence defence, cite the consistent line of authority (doc_032, doc_033, doc_025, doc_024) for pay-and-recover. Oppose any attempt to deduct compensation on licence grounds.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — This judgment is about a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes (carrying bricks/iron rods for construction). The insurer was exonerated because the vehicle was used for a purpose not covered by the policy. It has nothing to do with the driver's licence. The insurer cannot use it against a licence-defence claim.

doc_014 (Shivlal) — This judgment is about a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle under the 1939 Act. The insurer was exonerated because the risk of gratuitous passengers is not statutorily required to be covered. It has nothing to do with the driver's licence. Not relevant.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — This judgment is about passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire/reward. The court held they are not 'third parties' under the Act policy and pay-and-recover cannot be ordered. The ratio turns on the claimant's status (gratuitous passenger), not on licence defects. Our client is a genuine third party (pedestrian/other vehicle occupant), so this is distinguishable. The insurer cannot use it against a third-party claimant.

doc_030 (Dadapeera) — This judgment is about a person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor. The court held such a person is not a 'third party' entitled to pay-and-recover because the breach (travelling on mud-guard) is not one of the defences listed in Section 149(2). Critically, the court expressly notes that licence breach IS a defence under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) — 'a condition excluding driving by... any person who is not duly licensed.' So this judgment actually supports the proposition that where the breach IS a licence defect, pay-and-recover IS available. Not adverse.

doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal cases about rash and negligent driving. They address licence absence as a criminal offence under Section 181 MV Act but do not deal with insurance liability or compensation. Not relevant to the insurance defence.
